Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco

Assistant Professor · University of Zaragoza

My research addresses the robotic manipulation of deformable objects, in particular shape control: estimating the shape of an object from sensor data and computing the robot motions that drive it to a target shape.

I received my PhD from the University of Zaragoza in 2024 and was then a postdoctoral researcher at Institut Pascal (Clermont Auvergne INP), France. The thesis received three awards (CEA, SEIDROB–SPR and the University of Zaragoza) and was a finalist for the Georges Giralt PhD Award.

Research

I work on robotic manipulation along two lines: shape control of deformable objects and thermal servoing. In both, the robot motion is computed in closed loop from sensor measurements of the object (its shape or its surface temperature), with little or no model of the material.

Deformable object manipulation

Shape control: estimating the shape of an object from sensor data, establishing correspondences between its deformed configurations, and computing the robot motions that drive it to a target shape. I focus on robust, data-efficient methods and on coordinated manipulation with several robots.

Shape servoing tutorial Mini-game: Rod threading

Thermal servoing

Regulation of the temperature distribution of a surface with a robot-mounted heat source, as required in adhesive activation, composite curing or coating drying. Ergodic heat coverage control (EHCC) determines where to heat, by matching the time-averaged heat footprint of the source to the heat deficit of the surface, and how much, by adjusting the source-to-surface distance, without a thermal model of the material.

Interactive demos Mini-game: Dino egg incubator

Topics
Shape control, deformable-object manipulation, thermal servoing, robot perception and visual servoing.
Methods
Perception-to-manipulation pipelines, shape analysis, continuum mechanics, non-linear and ergodic control, and data-driven estimation and control.
Applications
Robotic manipulation, cooperative robotics and manufacturing, including the thermal processing of materials.

Interactive research demos

  • A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects Data-driven shape control of an elastic rod held by two robot arms.

I. Cuiral-Zueco and G. López-Nicolás, IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering, 2025.
  • Multiscale Procrustes-Based 3-D Shape Control 3D shape control of a deformable object with 6-DoF gripper actions computed by Procrustes analysis at multiple scales. I. Cuiral-Zueco and G. López-Nicolás, IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics, 2024.
  • Stereo Visual SLAM for Medical Endoscopy Stereo ORB-SLAM2 evaluated on laparoscopy sequences and extended with a dense tissue map built from stereo disparities.

Miscellany

People I admire

I’m not much of an extrovert in professional settings, but I think it’s nice to share a bit of what one enjoys. These are some people whose work I admire and often come back to.

  • 3Blue1Brown

    Grant Sanderson is a genius at explaining maths. His animated series on linear algebra, calculus and neural networks are worth watching more than once.

  • Veritasium

    Derek Muller and his team make some of the best science and engineering videos on YouTube, often built around an experiment or a common misconception.

  • braintruffle

    Torsten Heinze is a former nonlinear dynamics researcher and, frankly, a genius. His videos on fluids, chaos and control take 1,000 to 3,000 hours each, simulations included.

  • Zach Star

    Clever and often very funny maths and engineering videos.

  • Lemnismath

    One of the best maths channels in Spanish. Jaime covers paradoxes, fractals and the history of mathematics, and is building a computer out of marbles and wood.

  • Vulfpeck

    Minimalist funk band from Ann Arbor. Start with Dean Town and that Joe Dart bass line.

  • Snarky Puppy · Lingus

    Ten minutes from the album We Like It Here (2014), with Cory Henry’s famous keyboard solo towards the end.

  • David Bull · Slow woodblock printing

    An hour and a half of a master printmaker at work, one sheet after another, without cuts. Good for slowing down.

Educational robotics: LoCo CORP

I co-founded LoCo CORP, an initiative to update technology education in primary and secondary schools. We developed the Noctis and Aurel educational robots, together with workshops and courses based on them. In the workshops the robot was treated as a technical system rather than a toy: students worked on its electronics, programming and hardware design, with the aim of understanding the technology they use rather than only consuming it.

My main contribution was the LoCoVerso, a fictional setting in which the robots are newly discovered “species” on a remote planet. The narrative presented the technical lessons as scientific fieldwork, and students designed and customised new species (robots), combining the technical content with creative and artistic work.
